strengths: The paper addresses a relevant NLP evaluation problem: measuring changes in social bias after continued masked-language-model training. Distinguishing a model’s existing preferences from changes relative to its pretrained checkpoint is useful.

Experiments cover four accessible models, two established benchmarks, several existing measures, and detailed results across bias categories. Token-level examples help explain the proposed prediction-quality proxies.
Retraining on opposite sides of stereotype pairs provides a useful directional sanity check. The reported results support sensitivity of several measures to these interventions.
weaknesses: The central claim of superior bias-measurement accuracy is insufficiently validated. Retraining uses CPS, and evaluation reports the full CPS categories despite an 80/20 training/validation split; no independent evaluation is demonstrated. Consequently, the experiment cannot distinguish generalizable social bias from sentence memorization or lexical familiarity. Treating the retraining direction as ground truth for every category supports a sensitivity check, but stronger responses do not establish greater accuracy or justify calling other measures underestimates.

Human-annotation validation is weak and measures a different construct. Section 3.4.2 classifies whether sentence pairs express stereotypes, rather than independently assessing model bias. The best AUROCs are approximately 0.57; for RoBERTa, CRRA achieves 0.572 versus AUL’s 0.566. With 1,450 positive pairs, only 58 negative pairs, and no confidence intervals or significance tests for these differences, convincing superiority is not established. The procedure described as selecting thresholds to maximize AUROC also needs clarification.

BSRT has an unaddressed no-change case. Equation 10 returns zero when comparing identical models because every comparison is a tie, yet Section 3.5.2 interprets scores below 50 as a directional change. Unchanged margins therefore count alongside decreases. A tie-aware definition and a no-change control are needed, particularly for rank-based measures.

The statistical tests do not directly support the reported BSRT interpretation. Appendix P applies McNemar’s test to changes in binary stereotype preferences, whereas BSRT counts increases in preference margins. Margins can change without preferences switching signs. These significance markers therefore do not test BSRT’s departure from 50 or establish comparative measurement accuracy. Uncertainty across retraining runs is also unreported.

The added value of the proposed attention weighting remains unestablished. Previously proposed CRR already achieves the reported 100% directional-classification accuracy, as do unweighted ΔP and weighted ΔPA, while CRRA performs slightly worse. CRRA also changes the rank transformation alongside attention weighting, preventing attribution of its behavior to attention alone.

Reproducibility and methodological clarity require important revisions. The manuscript omits the learning rate, optimizer, batch size, seeds, exact split construction, and precise attention aggregation across layers and query/key dimensions. Although a package release is claimed, no identifiable package or repository link is supplied. Furthermore, the CSPS and SSS equations in Appendices B–C sum over all sentence tokens, conflicting with the modified/unmodified-token subsets described in the text. These ambiguities prevent verification of the implementation and baseline comparisons.
